title: Two pointers and sliding windows
lead: An Essential section on two pointers: indices that close in on a pair with a given sum, find 3SUM’s triples, merge two sorted lists, and bound windows of fixed and changing length. OI Wiki counts from 1 (num[1..n]), the 3SUM pseudocode from 0 (S[0..n−1]), the moving average by time (pn−k+1 … pn). 3SUM’s sort is a library call (Chapter 10) and its hash table Chapter 5’s. These windows keep a sum, product or count, never a hash set.
notes: OI Wiki’s code, its LeetCode statements, its second window example and its exercise lists, and the 3SUM article’s lead after its first sentence, are left out here.
exercise_notes: 3SUM and merging have no open exercise here: keon’s and TheAlgorithms’ versions are tests with no printed statement. TheAlgorithms’ two_pointer, max_sum_sliding_window and sliding_window, keon’s two_sum and longest_non_repeat, and tryalgo’s windows_k_distinct are left out for the same reason. The Kattis problems closestsums, cd, hothike and snowflakes and the ICPC problems tiredterry and slidecount publish only their sample tests. Merging two linked lists comes in Section 2.5 and Kattis kayaking in Chapter 6. Project Euler 8 has no published tests. The largest-series-product card asks for linear time, which Exercism does not, and the longest-substring card tests the cases icc’s solution notebook lists and a few more. The two MIT 6.006 cards are in this section’s NC file.

exercises.prompt:
Your task is to reverse a given string. Some examples:
  • Turn "stressed" into "desserts".
  • Turn "strops" into "sports".
  • Turn "racecar" into "racecar".

exercises.changes: The tests expect a ValueError for an empty series and for a length that is zero, negative or longer than the series.
exercises.prompt:
Given a string of digits, output all the contiguous substrings of length n in that string in the order that they appear. For example, the string "49142" has the following 3-digit series:
  • "491"
  • "914"
  • "142"
And the following 4-digit series:
  • "4914"
  • "9142"
And if you ask for a 6-digit series from a 5-digit string, you deserve whatever you get. Note that these series are only required to occupy adjacent positions in the input; the digits need not be numerically consecutive.

exercises.changes: A solution must run in time linear in the length of the input; the source asks for no bound. The tests expect a ValueError for a negative span, a span longer than the input and a character that is not a digit.
exercises.prompt:
Your task is to look for patterns in the long sequence of digits in the encrypted signal. The technique you're going to use here is called the largest series product. Let's define a few terms, first.
  • input: the sequence of digits that you need to analyze
  • series: a sequence of adjacent digits (those that are next to each other) that is contained within the input
  • span: how many digits long each series is
  • product: what you get when you multiply numbers together
Let's work through an example, with the input "63915".
  • To form a series, take adjacent digits in the original input.
  • If you are working with a span of 3, there will be three possible series:
    • "639"
    • "391"
    • "915"
  • Then we need to calculate the product of each series:
    • The product of the series "639" is 162 (6 × 3 × 9 = 162)
    • The product of the series "391" is 27 (3 × 9 × 1 = 27)
    • The product of the series "915" is 45 (9 × 1 × 5 = 45)
  • 162 is bigger than both 27 and 45, so the largest series product of "63915" is from the series "639". So the answer is 162.

exercises.changes: The tests call longest_substr(string, k), which the starter defines over your Solution class, and a string that is not a str raises a TypeError.
exercises.prompt:
Find the longest substring with at most k distinct characters.

Can we assume the inputs are valid? No.

Can we assume the strings are ASCII? Yes.

Is this case sensitive? Yes.

Is a substring a contiguous block of chars? Yes.

Do we expect an int as a result? Yes.

Can we assume this fits memory? Yes.

derivations.what: the next simple moving average from the previous one
derivations.source: Wikipedia, Moving average, Simple moving average

assumes.text: The previous mean is the mean over the last $k$ data points, $\textit{SMA}_{k,\text{prev}} = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i=n-k+1}^{n} p_{i}$.
The next mean is taken over the range from $n-k+2$ to $n+1$: $p_{n+1}$ comes in and $p_{n-k+1}$ drops out.
